/-!
# Erdős Problem 289
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/289](https://www.erdosproblems.com/289)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Asymptotics Filter Finset

namespace Erdos289

/-- Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $k$, there exist finite intervals
$I_1, \dotsc, I_k \subset \mathbb{N}$, distinct, not overlapping or adjacent, with
$|I_i| \geq 2$ for $1 \leq i \leq k$ such that
$$
1 = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{n \in I_i} \frac{1}{n}?
$$
Here two intervals are adjacent if their union is again an interval, so any two of the
$I_i$ must be separated by at least one integer.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_289 : answer(sorry) ↔
    (∀ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop, ∃ I : Fin k → ℕ × ℕ,
    (∀ i, (I i).1 < (I i).2) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → (I i).2 + 1 < (I j).1 ∨ (I j).2 + 1 < (I i).1) ∧
    ∑ i, ∑ n ∈ .Icc (I i).1 (I i).2, (n⁻¹ : ℚ) = 1) := by
  sorry

end Erdos289

reformulations.difference: The interval endpoints range over ℕ without explicit positivity, so Lean syntactically permits denominator 0, whose rational inverse is 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k ≥ 2, the remaining conditions force every lower endpoint to be positive. An interval starting at 0 has upper endpoint at least 1 and therefore contributes at least 1. Every other interval has strictly positive reciprocal sum, since its upper endpoint is positive. The total would then exceed 1, contradicting the required equality. Thus adding positivity leaves the witness condition unchanged for every k ≥ 2, and hence leaves the eventual-atTop statement unchanged. The exceptional witness [0,1] at k = 1 is irrelevant. The pointwise and eventual equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without using the problem theorem.
